items.stem: A high-volume ticket router classifies requests under a strict latency budget; the smallest model already clears the accuracy bar. A new certification mandate requires each classification carry an auditable rationale, not just a pass/fail score. Select the correct move.

opts.t: Move to a higher-capability model; only richer reasoning can produce the auditable rationale the certification mandate requires.
Keep the smallest model, since it already clears the accuracy bar the team benchmarked against.
Keep the smallest model, and add periodic manual audits of a sample of its classifications for compliance review.
Fine-tune the smallest model on tagged examples, without first testing whether a larger model already produces the required rationale.

items.whyRight: The mandate requires an auditable rationale for every classification, not just an accuracy score — a requirement the accuracy-bar test cannot verify. A bounded, high-volume classifier answers speed and cost; explaining its own reasoning at the standard a certification audit demands calls for a higher-capability model.

whyWrong.B: Clearing the accuracy bar answers a different question than the mandate asks; the stem states the requirement is an auditable rationale, which a pass/fail benchmark score does not provide.
whyWrong.C: Auditing a sample after the fact only detects gaps; the mandate requires an auditable rationale for every classification, produced up front, not discovered after deployment.
whyWrong.D: Fine-tuning is an expensive lever aimed at accuracy, not at producing the auditable rationale the mandate specifically requires; it doesn't test whether a larger model already meets it.

items.t1Clause: A new certification mandate requires each classification carry an auditable rationale, not just a pass/fail score.
items.factAnswerRaw: Move to a higher-capability model; only richer reasoning can produce the auditable rationale the certification mandate requires.

items.stem: A system prompt already blocks any refund mention outside business hours. A compliance officer holds written approval for after-hours refund reviews during fraud investigations; the boundary must hold for every other case before an audit. What should the team do?

opts.t: Reword the guardrail's refusal language to sound stricter, without changing what triggers it or where it lives.
Remove the guardrail and instead log every refund request for a reviewer to check afterward.
Configure the fraud-investigation exception as an environment variable the operations team can toggle during audits.
Add a scoped exception for the approved fraud-investigation case directly into the system-prompt guardrail, leaving the boundary intact elsewhere.

items.whyRight: The guardrail's location is already correct — the fix is to narrow what it blocks, not where it lives. Writing the approved fraud-investigation exception directly into the system-prompt guardrail preserves its authority everywhere else while accommodating the one case leadership has actually authorized.

whyWrong.A: Rewording the refusal language changes nothing about which requests it blocks; the approved fraud-investigation case would still be refused exactly as before.
whyWrong.B: Removing the guardrail drops preventive enforcement entirely; a reviewer checking logs afterward cannot stop an unauthorized refund before it happens.
whyWrong.C: Environment variables are deploy-time infrastructure configuration; they never reach the model, so the exception would have no effect on its actual behavior.

items.t1Clause: a compliance officer holds written approval for an after-hours fraud-investigation exception
items.factAnswerRaw: Add a scoped exception for the approved fraud-investigation case directly into the system-prompt guardrail, leaving the boundary intact elsewhere.

items.stem: A high-volume support-formatting feature inconsistently applies one output format despite clear instructions, with one sprint left before launch. A colleague proposes adding twelve examples covering formats the model already handles correctly. What should the team do?

opts.t: Add the twelve examples as proposed; broader example coverage reinforces the model's formatting behavior overall.
Rewrite the system prompt instructions to state the formatting rule in even more explicit language.
Replace the twelve examples with four to six examples targeted at the exact case that keeps failing.
Add all twelve examples now for thoroughness, and add targeted ones later only if the case still fails.

items.whyRight: The failure is a targeting problem, not a volume problem. Twelve examples of cases the model already handles correctly never touch the one case still failing; four to six examples built from that exact failing case fix the ambiguity examples exist to resolve.

whyWrong.A: More examples do not help if they cover cases the model already gets right; the twelve as proposed never address the one case that keeps failing.
whyWrong.B: Instructions have already failed to produce consistent output; rewording them again doesn't fix a precision problem that targeted examples are built to solve.
whyWrong.D: Adding volume now and targeting later reverses the order that fixes the failure; the twelve broad examples spend the sprint's budget without touching the actual case.

items.t1Clause: covering formats the model already handles correctly

items.stem: A support agent's per-turn latency and token cost climb steadily as a conversation passes fifty turns, even though each response stays about the same length, threatening a per-session cost cap. An engineer blames Claude's memory buffer filling up internally. What is the actual cause?

opts.t: The context window is being exceeded this early in a fifty-turn conversation.
Claude retains an internal memory buffer across calls that grows heavier with each additional turn.
The model is generating progressively longer, more detailed responses as the conversation continues.
The application resends the full conversation history on every call, so token volume grows with each additional turn.

items.whyRight: The API is stateless: nothing about the conversation persists on Claude's side between calls. Every request must resend the complete history, so as a conversation lengthens, the resent history itself grows — explaining rising per-call token volume, latency, and cost with no change in response length.

whyWrong.A: A fifty-turn conversation is far below any context-window limit; exceeding it cannot explain a steady rise from this early stage.
whyWrong.B: Claude's API is stateless and keeps no memory buffer between calls; nothing about the model's internals accumulates across turns at all.
whyWrong.C: The stem states each response stays about the same length, which rules out response length as the driver of the rising cost.

items.t1Clause: even though each response stays about the same length

notes: g13 (2.2, S8-inverted, anchor F-2.2-01): CONFIRMS Paper 2's g14/g15 IRREDUCIBLE finding. Section 2.2's core rule (system prompt is the only durable-authority location) is absolute -- its three wrong mechanisms (first-message placement, env var, detective logging-after-removal) are unconditionally wrong, never correct under any other section-2.2 row, so no clause deletion/inversion in the stem makes A/B/C become correct. t1Clause/t1Alt (invert the 'written approval' clause -> t1Alt A) is a best-effort attempt only and does NOT cleanly resolve to a distinct, nameable section-2.2 decision-table row; T2 (neighbour-correct distractor) is similarly unreachable within this section's own table for the same structural reason. The item's correct answer itself ('add a scoped exception in place, don't relocate/remove the guardrail') is still genuinely distinct in text from F-2.2-01's own answer ('System prompt') and is the most defensible S8 construction found -- recommend the grounding audit confirm IRREDUCIBLE status for T1/T2 on this item specifically, not reject the item outright.

g14 and g15 (misconception-unit items, sections 2.3 and 2.5): T1 resolves cleanly on both (clean clause inversions with real corpus-table t1Alts). T2 (neighbour-correct distractor) was only partially achievable -- both sections' decision tables are thin and directionally uniform (2.3's 'add examples' answer is always about targeting, never volume; 2.5's root-cause rows have only one correct mechanism each), so no wrong option in either item is literally 'correct in a neighbouring situation' within the same section's table. Distractors were instead built from each section's explicitly-listed wrong mechanisms. Flagging for the grounding audit's awareness, not as a rejection.
